extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy, policymakers, and general readers interested in law, property, and socialism
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical essay arguing for a narrow, negative role of law (to prevent injustice and secure rights) and defining/condemning 'legal plunder' and legislative overreach, with historical examples and critiques of socialist and classical legislative doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three solutions to legal plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only three solutions: (1) When the few plunder the many. (2) When everybody plunders everybody else. (3) When nobody plunders anybody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are mutually exclusive outcomes produced by the law: partial plunder (elective privilege partial), universal plunder (elective privilege universal / socialism/communism), or absence of plunder (principle of justice). Evaluate political programs by which of these legal outcomes they tend to produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law's proper aim — 'LAW IS ORGANISED JUSTICE' / prevent injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: The true solution of the social problem is contained in the words 'LAW IS ORGANISED JUSTICE.' More precisely, 'the aim of the law is to prevent injustice from reigning' — to secure to every one his right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the law as having a negative, defensive function: its necessary sanction is force, but it should be used only to secure rights and prevent injustices, not to reorganise society positively. Any extension beyond securing rights risks perverting law and turning force against right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: Plunder: when a portion of wealth passes out of the hands of him who has acquired it, without his consent, and without compensation, to him who has not created it, whether by force or by artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this scientific/precise sense when judging policies: transfers effected by law that meet this definition are 'plunder.' If the law itself effects the transfer, it is 'legal plunder' and is socially more dangerous because society and the lawgiver become responsible rather than an individual wrongdoer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law must not organise human activities (no positive organisation by force)
rubrics_metrics.description: To organise justice by law excludes the idea of organising by law, or by force any manifestation whatever of human activity—labour, charity, agriculture, commerce, industry, instruction, the fine arts, or religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any law that imposes specific forms, methods, or subjects of labour, instruction, worship, or other activities substitutes the legislator's will for individual will, violating personality, liberty, and property. Such positive organisation by law should be rejected as it 'organises injustice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Law's domain is limited by force — law's negative/defensive role
rubrics_metrics.description: Law is force, and consequently the domain of the law cannot lawfully extend beyond the domain of force. When law and force keep a man within the bounds of justice, they impose nothing upon him but a mere negation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposed legal powers by whether they require positive imposition (beyond preventing harm). If a law compels individuals into particular actions or institutions rather than merely preventing harm, it exceeds the legitimate domain of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: False philanthropy as a root of legal plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal plunder has two roots: one in human egotism; the other in false philanthropy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of benevolent-sounding reforms (fraternity, solidarity, organisation) that seek to use law to redistribute or impose collective welfare; regardless of intentions, if they create uncompensated transfers they are legal plunder and undermine liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of legal plunder / instruments of organised injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection of tariffs, prizes for encouragement, right to profit, right to labour, right to assistance, right to instruction, progressive taxation, gratuitousness of credit, social workshops — these contain the principle of plunder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these concrete policy examples as tests: if a measure requires compulsory transfer or privilege captured by some at the expense of others without consent/compensation, it is to be classified as legal plunder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law is not a self-supplied fountain — limits in addressing inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: The law is not a self-supplied fountain. Nothing can enter the public treasury in favour of one citizen or one class but what other citizens and other classes have been forced to send to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies promising public provision must be assessed for who is being forced to pay; equalisation by law necessarily takes from some to give to others (plunder) unless citizens only receive back their exact contribution. Thus rightful legal action cannot create prosperity out of nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-imposed education, religion, and morality violate liberty/property
rubrics_metrics.description: When the law, through force, imposes a form of labour, a method or a subject of instruction, a creed, or a worship, it acts positively upon men and violates liberty and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between allowing voluntary transactions (teachers and learners contracting freely) and coercing education/religion by the State. The latter is an unjust use of force and should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish voluntary association from forced/ legal fraternity
rubrics_metrics.description: What we repudiate is not natural organisation, but forced organisation. It is not free association, but the forms of association which they would impose upon us. It is not spontaneous fraternity, but legal fraternity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating proposals framed in terms like 'fraternity' or 'solidarity,' insist on whether the association is voluntary or legally enforced; legal enforcement of association displaces responsibility and is equivalent to organised injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socialist conflation of Government and society criticized
rubrics_metrics.description: Socialism confounds Government and society; every time we object to a thing being done by Government, it concludes that we object to its being done at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess arguments that equate state action with social action: critique them by separating social (private/voluntary) solutions from governmental/compulsory solutions and by warning that rejecting state provision is not rejecting the underlying social goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politicians' presumption: viewing people as passive material to be shaped
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern politicians, particularly Socialists, suppose that men are devoid of any principle of action and are inert matter, passive particles susceptible of receiving from an exterior will an infinite number of forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate regulatory or planning schemes by questioning the presumption that citizens lack initiative or judgment. Programs that assume large-scale social shaping by legislation overlook human agency and are likely to fail or cause injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against experimenting on human populations as if they were machines
rubrics_metrics.description: Socialists often propose 'trying all systems' and even demand a parish and its inhabitants to experiment upon; the distance between the inventor and his machine is immeasurable compared to the relation between legislator and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat proposals to conduct social experiments through coercive legislation with great skepticism: human societies are not laboratory specimens, and forced experiments risk grave injustices and unintended harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical-warning criterion — lessons from classical writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical writers (Bossuet, Fenelon, Montesquieu, Rousseau, Raynal, Mably, Condillac) often depicted lawgivers as shaping passive peoples; these examples show a recurring tendency to overestimate the legislator's role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical examples as cautionary evidence: the tradition of exalted legislators should not be taken as justification for modern legal overreach. Scrutinize claims of the legislator's capacity to mould society and prefer solutions respecting individual responsibility.
